title: Unbiased estimator
body: An estimator is unbiased if, on average, its value does not underestimate or overestimate the population parameter.
ced_evidence: 3.1.A.1 "an estimator is unbiased if, on average, the value of the estimator does not underestimate or overestimate the population parameter"

title: Point estimator
body: A sample statistic is a point estimator of the corresponding population parameter; for example, the sample proportion \hat{p} is a point estimator for the population proportion p.
ced_evidence: 3.1.B.1 "A sample statistic is a point estimator of the corresponding population parameter"

title: Mean of the sampling distribution of a sample proportion
body: \mu_{\hat{p}} = p
ced_evidence: 3.2.A.1 "mean \mu_{\hat p} = p"

title: Standard deviation of the sampling distribution of a sample proportion
body: \sigma_{\hat{p}} = \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}
caution: This requires the sampled values to be independent and uses the population proportion p, not \hat{p}.
ced_evidence: 3.2.A.1 "when the sampled values are independent... standard deviation"

title: Conditions for the sampling distribution of \hat{p}
body: Conditions for using the sampling distribution of a sample proportion: randomization, 10%, and a large enough sample size.

items.label: Randomization
items.meaning: The data should be collected using a random sample.

items.label: 10% condition
items.meaning: When sampling without replacement, the population size must be at least 10 times the sample size: n \le 10%N.

items.label: Large sample size
items.meaning: np \ge 10 and n(1-p) \ge 10, the expected numbers of successes and failures.

title: Interpret sampling distribution results in context
body: The mean, standard deviation, and probabilities of a sampling distribution of a sample proportion must be interpreted in the context of a specific population.
ced_evidence: 3.2.C.1 "interpreted in the context of a specific population"

title: Confidence interval
body: A confidence interval is an interval estimate for a population parameter, calculated from a sample, so it may or may not contain the parameter's value.
ced_evidence: 3.3.A.1 "A confidence interval is an interval estimate for a population parameter"

title: Critical value z*
body: The critical value z* is such that -z* and z* bound the middle C% of the standard normal distribution, where C% is the confidence level.
ced_evidence: 3.3.C.1 "z denotes a critical value, such that z and -z represent the boundaries enclosing the middle C%"

title: Identify the procedure and parameter for one proportion
body: The procedure is a one-sample z-interval for a population proportion, and the parameter must name the proportion, the response variable, and the population in context.
ced_evidence: 3.3.A.1, 3.3.A.2 "should reference the proportion, the response variable, and the population in context"

title: Conditions for a one-sample z-interval for p
body: A one-sample z-interval for a population proportion requires three conditions.

items.label: Randomization
items.meaning: The data should be collected using a random sample.

items.label: 10% condition
items.meaning: When sampling without replacement, n \le 10%N.

items.label: Normality
items.meaning: The observed numbers of successes n\hat{p} and failures n(1-\hat{p}) are each at least 10.

caution: The interval condition uses observed counts from \hat{p}; the test of one proportion uses np_0 and n(1-p_0).

title: One-sample z-interval for a population proportion
body: \hat{p} \pm z^{*}\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}}
ced_evidence: 3.3.C.2 "point estimate ± (margin of error)"

title: Standard error of a sample proportion
body: SE_{\hat{p}} = \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}}
ced_evidence: 3.3.D.1 "standard error (SE) of a statistic is an estimate of the standard deviation of the sampling distribution"

title: Margin of error for a proportion
body: MOE = z^{*}\cdot SE_{\hat{p}} = z^{*}\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}}
ced_evidence: 3.3.D.3 "margin of error of \hat p is half the width of the confidence interval"

title: Minimum sample size for a given margin of error
body: n = \left(\frac{z^{*}}{MOE}\right)^{2}\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})
caution: If \hat{p} is not available, use 0.5 to get the upper bound on the required sample size.
ced_evidence: 3.3.D.4 "use p = 0.5 in order to find the upper bound for the sample size"

title: Standard error
body: The standard error quantifies the typical amount that a statistic will vary from the value of the corresponding population parameter.
ced_evidence: 3.3.D.2 "quantifies the typical amount that a statistic will vary"

title: Interpreting the confidence level
body: In repeated random sampling with the same sample size, approximately C% of the confidence intervals calculated will capture the population proportion.
caution: The confidence level describes the long-run capture rate of the method, not the probability that one computed interval contains the parameter.
ced_evidence: 3.4.A.2 "approximately C% of confidence intervals calculated will capture the population proportion"

title: Interpreting a C% confidence interval
body: Say "We are C% confident that the interval (a, b) contains the true value of the parameter," naming the parameter and population in context.
ced_evidence: 3.4.A.3 "we are C% confident that the interval (a, b) contains the true value of the parameter"

title: Justify a claim from a confidence interval
body: A confidence interval gives a range of plausible values for the parameter, and a claim is supported when the claimed value is among those values.
ced_evidence: 3.4.B.1 "provides a range of plausible values that may serve as convincing evidence"

title: Effect of increasing the confidence level (same sample)
body: For a given sample, raising the confidence level changes three quantities, all in the same direction.

items.label: Critical value
items.meaning: Increases.

items.label: Margin of error
items.meaning: Increases.

items.label: Interval width
items.meaning: Increases.

title: Sample size and interval width
body: Increasing the sample size decreases the standard error, so the interval width tends to decrease and is approximately proportional to 1/\sqrt{n}.
ced_evidence: 3.4.C.2 "approximately proportional to 1/\sqrt{n}"

title: Null and alternative hypotheses
body: The null hypothesis H0 is the status quo statement about a parameter, assumed correct unless there is convincing evidence otherwise; the alternative Ha is the claim for which evidence is being collected.
ced_evidence: 3.5.B.1 "null hypothesis, H0, is the statement about a parameter that is assumed to be correct"

title: Hypotheses for a one-sample z-test for p
body: H_0: p = p_0 with Ha one-sided (p < p_0 or p > p_0) or two-sided (p \ne p_0); the test is run at the boundary of equality and the parameter is described in context.
caution: Write hypotheses with the parameter p, not a statistic or undefined symbol, and define p with its population.

title: Conditions for a one-sample z-test for p
body: A one-sample z-test for a population proportion requires three conditions.

items.label: Randomization
items.meaning: The data should be collected using a random sample.

items.label: 10% condition
items.meaning: When sampling without replacement, n \le 10%N.

items.label: Normality
items.meaning: The expected numbers of successes np_0 and failures n(1-p_0) are each at least 10.

caution: The test uses the null value p_0, not \hat{p}, in the normality condition.

title: p-value
body: The p-value is the probability of obtaining a test statistic as extreme or more extreme (in the direction of Ha) than the one observed, given that the null hypothesis is true.
ced_evidence: 3.6.A.1 "probability of obtaining a test statistic as extreme or more extreme"

title: p-value by direction of the alternative (z-test)
body: The p-value is found in the tail(s) of the null distribution indicated by Ha.

items.label: Ha: >
items.meaning: P(z \ge x), the probability at or above the observed test statistic.

items.label: Ha: <
items.meaning: P(z \le x), the probability at or below the observed test statistic.

items.label: Ha: \ne
items.meaning: P(z \le -|x|) + P(z \ge |x|), both tails.

title: Simulated p-value
body: If the test statistic's distribution is simulated, the p-value is the proportion of simulated values in the null distribution as extreme or more extreme than the observed value, in the direction of Ha.
ced_evidence: 3.6.A.2 "the p-value is the proportion of values in the null distribution that are as extreme or more extreme"

title: Interpreting a p-value
body: An interpretation must state that the p-value is computed assuming the null hypothesis is true, in context.
ced_evidence: 3.6.A.3 "computed by assuming the null hypothesis is true"

title: Small versus not-small p-values
body: A small p-value means the observed statistic would be unusual if H0 were true and provides evidence for Ha; a p-value that is not small gives no convincing evidence for Ha and is not evidence that H0 is true.
ced_evidence: 3.6.A.4, 3.6.A.5 "nor do they provide evidence that the null hypothesis is true"

title: Test statistic for a one-sample z-test for p
body: z = \frac{\hat{p} - p_0}{\sqrt{\frac{p_0(1-p_0)}{n}}}
ced_evidence: 3.7.A.1 "The test statistic for testing a population proportion"

title: Significance level
body: The significance level \alpha is the predetermined probability of rejecting the null hypothesis given that it is true.
ced_evidence: 3.7.B.1 "predetermined probability of rejecting the null hypothesis given that it is true"

title: Decision rule comparing p-value to \alpha
body: If the p-value \le \alpha, reject H0; if the p-value > \alpha, fail to reject H0.
ced_evidence: 3.7.B.2 "If the p-value ≤ α, then reject the null hypothesis"

title: Conclusion wording for a hypothesis test
body: State the conclusion in context, in terms of Ha, with non-definitive language, referencing the parameter and population; never conclude H0 is true or proven.
caution: Say "convincing statistical evidence" or "not convincing evidence," never "accept H0" or "prove."
ced_evidence: 3.7.B.4, 3.7.B.6 "using non-definitive language"

title: Type I error
body: A Type I error occurs when there is convincing evidence that Ha is true (small p-value) but it is not, i.e., rejecting a true H0.
ced_evidence: 3.8.A.1 "convincing statistical evidence that the alternative hypothesis is true... but it is not"

title: Type II error
body: A Type II error occurs when there is not convincing evidence that Ha is true (large p-value) but it is true, i.e., failing to reject a false H0.
ced_evidence: 3.8.A.2 "not convincing statistical evidence that the alternative hypothesis is true"

title: Power of a test
body: The power of a hypothesis test is the probability that it correctly rejects a false null hypothesis.
ced_evidence: 3.8.A.3 "probability that a hypothesis test will correctly reject the false null hypothesis"

title: Probabilities of Type I and Type II errors
body: P(\text{Type I error}) = \alpha, \qquad P(\text{Type II error}) = 1 - \text{power}
ced_evidence: 3.8.B.1, 3.8.B.2 "probability of making a Type II error is 1 − power"

title: Factors that decrease P(Type II) and increase power
body: Each of these increases power (others held fixed).

items.label: Sample size
items.meaning: Sample size(s) increase.

items.label: Standard error
items.meaning: Standard error decreases.

items.label: True parameter
items.meaning: True parameter value is farther from the null value.

items.label: Significance level
items.meaning: \alpha of the test increases.

title: Consequences of errors guide design choices
body: The consequences of a Type I error influence the choice of \alpha, and the consequences of a Type II error influence how large the sample size should be.

title: Mean of the sampling distribution of \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2
ced_evidence: 3.9.A.1 "mean, \mu_{\hat p_1 - \hat p_2}"

title: Standard deviation of the sampling distribution of \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2
ced_evidence: 3.9.A.1 "standard deviation" for two independent populations

title: Conditions for the sampling distribution of \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2
body: Conditions for an approximately normal sampling distribution of a difference in sample proportions.

items.label: Randomization
items.meaning: Two independent random samples; for an experiment, treatments randomly assigned to experimental units.

items.label: 10% condition
items.meaning: n_1 \le 10%N_1 and n_2 \le 10%N_2 when sampling without replacement.

items.label: Large samples
items.meaning: n_1p_1, n_1(1-p_1), n_2p_2, n_2(1-p_2) are all at least 10.

title: Identify the procedure and parameter for a difference of proportions
body: The procedure is a two-sample z-interval for a difference between population proportions, and the parameter names the difference in proportions, the response variable, and the populations in context.

title: Conditions for a two-sample z-interval for p1 − p2
body: A two-sample z-interval for a difference between proportions requires three conditions.

items.label: Randomization
items.meaning: Two independent random samples or a randomized experiment.

items.label: 10% condition
items.meaning: n_1 \le 10%N_1 and n_2 \le 10%N_2 when sampling without replacement; unnecessary for a randomized experiment.

items.label: Normality
items.meaning: Observed successes and failures in both samples, n_1\hat{p}_1, n_1(1-\hat{p}_1), n_2\hat{p}_2, n_2(1-\hat{p}_2), are all at least 10.

title: Two-sample z-interval for a difference of proportions
ced_evidence: 3.10.C.2 "interval estimate for the difference between two population proportions"

title: Standard error of \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2
ced_evidence: 3.10.D.1 "standard error (SE) for the difference between two population proportions"

title: Margin of error for a difference of proportions
body: MOE = z^{*}\cdot SE_{\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2}
ced_evidence: 3.10.D.2 "critical value z times the standard error"

title: Interpreting a confidence interval for p1 − p2
body: Say "We are C% confident that the interval (a, b) contains the difference between the population proportions," naming the parameter and both populations in context.
ced_evidence: 3.11.A.3 "we are C% confident that the interval (a, b) contains the parameter for the difference"

title: Claim about a difference from an interval and 0
body: If the interval contains 0 there is insufficient evidence of a difference between the population proportions; if it does not contain 0 there is sufficient evidence of a difference.
ced_evidence: 3.11.B.1 "if the interval contains 0, then there is insufficient evidence"

title: Hypotheses for a two-sample z-test for p1 − p2
body: H_0: p_1 = p_2 (or p_1 - p_2 = 0) with Ha p_1 > p_2, p_1 < p_2, or p_1 \ne p_2 (equivalently, difference >, <, \ne 0); parameters are named with populations in context.
ced_evidence: 3.12.B.1 "null hypothesis indicates no difference"; 3.12.A.1-2

title: Combined (pooled) proportion
body: \hat{p}_c = \frac{n_1\hat{p}_1 + n_2\hat{p}_2}{n_1 + n_2}
caution: The pooled proportion is used for the test (assuming H0 true), not for the confidence interval.
ced_evidence: 3.12.C.1.iii "combined (or pooled) proportion assuming that H0 is true"

title: Conditions for a two-sample z-test for p1 − p2
body: A two-sample z-test for a difference between proportions requires three conditions.

items.label: Randomization
items.meaning: Two independent random samples or a randomized experiment.

items.label: 10% condition
items.meaning: n_1 \le 10%N_1 and n_2 \le 10%N_2 when sampling without replacement; unnecessary for a randomized experiment.

items.label: Normality
items.meaning: n_1\hat{p}_c, n_1(1-\hat{p}_c), n_2\hat{p}_c, n_2(1-\hat{p}_c) are all at least 10.

caution: The test's normality condition uses the pooled \hat{p}_c, unlike the interval's use of each \hat{p}_i.

title: Test statistic for a two-sample z-test for p1 − p2
body: z = \frac{(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) - 0}{\sqrt{\hat{p}_c(1-\hat{p}_c)\left(\frac{1}{n_1}+\frac{1}{n_2}\right)}}
ced_evidence: 3.13.A.1 "The test statistic for the difference between two population proportions"

title: Chi-square statistic
body: The chi-square statistic measures the distance between observed and expected counts relative to expected counts.
ced_evidence: 3.14.A.1 "measures the distance between observed and expected counts relative to expected counts"

title: Shape of chi-square distributions
body: Chi-square distributions take only positive values and are skewed right, with the skew less pronounced as degrees of freedom increase.
ced_evidence: 3.14.A.2 "positive values and are skewed right"

title: Homogeneity versus independence
body: Use a chi-square test for homogeneity to compare the distributions of one categorical variable across two or more populations or treatments; use a test for independence to ask whether two categorical variables are associated in a single population.

title: Hypotheses for chi-square tests
body: Homogeneity: H0 is no difference in the distributions of the categorical variable across populations or treatments, Ha is a difference. Independence: H0 is no association (independent) between the two categorical variables in the population, Ha is an association.
caution: Reference the variables and the population(s) in context.

title: Conditions for a chi-square test
body: A chi-square test for homogeneity or independence requires three conditions.

items.label: Randomization
items.meaning: Independence: a random sample. Homogeneity: independent random samples or a randomized experiment.

items.label: 10% condition
items.meaning: When sampling without replacement, n \le 10%N; unnecessary for a randomized experiment.

items.label: Expected counts
items.meaning: All expected counts should be greater than 5.

caution: Check expected counts, not observed counts. The unit overview words the threshold as "at least 5", while 3.14.D.1.iii says "greater than 5".
ced_evidence: 3.14.D.1.i-iii "all expected counts should be greater than 5"

title: Expected count in a two-way table
body: \text{expected count} = \frac{(\text{row total})(\text{column total})}{\text{table total}}
ced_evidence: 3.15.A.1 "expected count = row total · column total / total table"

title: Chi-square test statistic
body: \chi^{2} = \sum \frac{(\text{Observed} - \text{Expected})^{2}}{\text{Expected}}
caution: The sum is taken over all cells of the two-way table.
ced_evidence: 3.15.B.1 "chi-square statistic"

title: Degrees of freedom for a chi-square test
body: df = (\text{number of rows} - 1)(\text{number of columns} - 1)
ced_evidence: 3.15.B.1 "degrees of freedom equal to (number of rows − 1)(number of columns − 1)"

title: Chi-square conclusion
body: Reject H0 if the p-value \le \alpha and fail to reject if the p-value > \alpha, stating the conclusion in context in terms of Ha with non-definitive language and a reference to the population(s).
ced_evidence: 3.15.D.1, 3.15.D.3 "using non-definitive language"
